questions.q: What is the purpose of the kid (Key ID) parameter in a JWT header?
o: It names the user who originally issued the token on the client
It tells the server which key file to load for signature checks
It encodes the expiration date in a compact header-only format
It identifies the JWT specification version the client supports
questions.x: kid is a header hint the server uses to pick the right verification key when several keys exist, for example during rotation. This lab treats that value as a filesystem path.
questions.h: Servers can have more than one signing key. kid answers which key should be used for this token.

questions.q: In this lab, where does the server look up the key identified by kid?
o: A remote JWKS endpoint hosted on an external content CDN
A PostgreSQL table that maps kid values to stored HMAC secrets
The local filesystem, using kid as a path to the key file
An in-memory map of keys populated once at process startup
questions.x: The server builds a disk path from the kid value and reads that file. If kid contains ../ sequences, the path can escape the intended key directory.
questions.h: The attack is called path traversal. What kind of resource is reached with ../ in a path?

questions.q: Why is /dev/null the ideal kid target in this attack?
o: Reading it crashes the kernel and disables all auth checks
It returns no bytes, so the HMAC secret is an empty string
It prints the real signing key in an error message to the client
World-readable permissions let any process dump the stored secret
questions.x: On Linux, /dev/null always returns zero bytes when read. The server therefore uses an empty HMAC key. Signing with the same empty string makes both sides match.
questions.h: The attacker must know the key the server will use. Which file always has completely predictable empty content?

questions.q: Which kid path is used to walk from an unknown directory up to /dev/null?
o: /root/dev/null, which is assumed to be the device from any dir
../dev/null, which jumps to the device from the working directory
../../../../../../dev/null, which walks up until the device
%2Fdev%2Fnull, which URL-decodes and skips directory checks
questions.x: Each ../ goes up one directory. A long chain reaches the filesystem root regardless of starting depth. Linux clamps paths at root, so extra ../ sequences are harmless.
questions.h: A single ../ goes up one level. If the key directory depth is unknown, how many ../ segments make reaching root likely?

questions.q: After pointing kid at /dev/null, how is the forged token signed?
o: RS256 with a newly generated RSA private key the attacker owns
HS256 with an empty string as the HMAC secret on both sides
HS512 with the literal string null read from the device name
The none algorithm, sending a two-part token with no signature
questions.x: The server still uses HS256 and reads the key from /dev/null, getting empty bytes. The attacker signs with HS256 and an empty string so the HMAC matches.
questions.h: The server's key file returns nothing. What HMAC secret matches a key that is empty?

questions.q: Which of the following is true of this lab's kid path traversal attack?
o: kid is concatenated into a filesystem path without sanitization
Pointing kid at /dev/null prints the real HMAC secret
All of these statements are true about this kid traversal lab
The forged token is signed with RS256 and the public key
questions.x: kid is concatenated into a filesystem path without sanitization, which is the bug. /dev/null returns empty content, not the real secret. The forge uses HS256 with an empty string, not RS256. All is wrong because those last two claims are false.
questions.h: How does this server turn kid into a key? Does it look up a database row, or open a file path?

questions.q: What makes kid path traversal possible in the server code?
o: The JWT library ships a known CVE for unsanitized kid lookups
The server concatenates kid into a path without validating it
kid is optional, so the server skips all validation on that field
Filesystem ACLs are misconfigured and allow world-writable keys
questions.x: The bug is unsanitized concatenation into a file path. If kid is ../../../../../../../dev/null, the resolved path leaves the intended key directory.
questions.h: The server builds a filesystem path from a value it did not validate. What happens if that value contains ../ ?

questions.q: Which defense most directly stops this kid filesystem attack?
o: Encrypt the JWT so the kid value cannot be read by an attacker
Allowlist known key identifiers before using kid in any path
Switch to RS256 so keys are never read from disk in any case
Rate-limit requests so traversal probes cannot finish in time
questions.x: An allowlist compares kid to known identifiers and rejects anything else before a file is opened. Encrypting the token does not help, because the attacker issues their own token.
questions.h: The server should not accept a kid it never issued. What validation pattern rejects values not on a pre-approved list?

questions.q: Which of these kid values would a strict allowlist correctly reject?
o: key-2026-01, a dated identifier for the current signing key
prod-primary, a name for the live production HMAC secret file
../../../../../../dev/null, a traversal to an empty device
rsa-v2, a short identifier used during an RSA key rotation
questions.x: The traversal string is not a real key identifier. An allowlist that only accepts known names such as key-2026-01 or prod-primary would reject it before any disk read.
questions.h: Which option looks like a filesystem traversal attempt rather than a normal key identifier?

questions.q: Why does locking down the real key file not stop this attack?
o: Secure key storage fully prevents kid path traversal attacks
The lookup is redirected to /dev/null, ignoring the stored key
Secure storage slows the attack but still leaks the real secret
The attack only works when keys live in environment variables
questions.x: The attack does not steal the real key. It points key lookup at a file with known empty content. Protecting the legitimate key is irrelevant if the path can be hijacked.
questions.h: The attack replaces the key path instead of reading the stored secret. Does hardening that original file stop the substitution?
